entry.title: Introducing SolariumDB: Taking Control of the Storage Layer in .NET
entry.summary: SolariumDB is an embedded key-value storage engine written entirely in C#, built to give CamusDB end-to-end control of the storage layer in .NET.
entry.content:
What if you could debug your database's storage engine with the same tools you use to debug your .NET applications? Or optimize how it writes to disk for your specific workload?

That's the motivation behind SolariumDB, an embedded key-value database written entirely in C#.

SolariumDB brings us one step closer to building a database entirely in .NET, from the SQL layer down to the code responsible for organizing files and writing data to disk.

Why Build Another Storage Engine?​

SolariumDB is different from CamusDB. It isn't a distributed SQL database or a standalone database server. It operates at a much lower level: the storage engine.

This is the layer responsible for persisting data, organizing files, managing memory, and recovering after failures.

SolariumDB follows the architecture of RocksDB, using a Log-Structured Merge Tree (LSM-tree) with write-ahead logs, memtables, SSTables, and background compaction.

RocksDB is an incredibly mature and reliable storage engine. It's the default backend for CamusDB, and we have no plans to change that anytime soon.

However, from a .NET application's perspective, RocksDB can feel like a black box.

When investigating a performance problem, we can profile our C# code, but following an operation into the native storage engine requires a different set of tools.

We also have limited control over its internal I/O behavior without modifying RocksDB itself.

SolariumDB changes that.

Owning the Entire Stack​

By implementing the storage engine in C#, we gain several important advantages:

  • End-to-end debugging and profiling. We can follow an operation from the application down to the storage layer using .NET tools.
  • Direct control over I/O. Every file operation goes through an abstraction we control, allowing us to experiment with Linux io_uring and different I/O strategies.
  • Workload-specific optimizations. We can optimize storage behavior around the applications using it rather than relying exclusively on general-purpose defaults.
  • Better observability. We can expose internal metrics such as write stalls, pending compactions, memtable usage, and file activity.
  • No native dependencies. The storage engine can be distributed as .NET assemblies without maintaining separate native binaries for different platforms.

These benefits aren't purely theoretical.

SolariumDB was initially designed around the Raft log of Kommander and also serves as a storage backend for Kahuna.

For example, Raft logs are mostly append-only and periodically discard old entries. SolariumDB can move non-overlapping SSTables between levels without rewriting their contents, reducing unnecessary disk I/O.

This is the kind of optimization that becomes easier when we control the storage engine.

What About Performance?​

One of my biggest questions was whether a storage engine written in C# could compete with RocksDB.

The early results have been encouraging.

In our October 29 benchmarks, SolariumDB achieved up to 2.8 times RocksDB's throughput in unsynced Kommander WAL workloads, while synced writes generally performed similarly because both engines were limited by the storage device.

In Kahuna's larger, page-cached dataset, SolariumDB also achieved approximately 1.8 times the read throughput of RocksDB configured to use buffered reads with eight reader threads.

These results come from specific workloads on a single machine, not a claim that SolariumDB is universally faster.

There are still areas to improve. Garbage collection can affect tail latency under heavy load, some compaction workloads need better tuning, and the io_uring implementation doesn't outperform the default I/O path in every scenario.

But the results demonstrate something important: writing a storage engine in C# doesn't automatically mean sacrificing competitive performance.

The complete methodology and results are available in our benchmarks.

Different Workloads, Different Storage Engines​

CamusDB was designed to support multiple storage backends, following a philosophy similar to MySQL, where different storage engines can be selected for different requirements.

Some workloads prioritize write throughput, others need efficient range scans, and others require predictable latency under heavy concurrency.

Having interchangeable storage engines gives us the flexibility to explore those tradeoffs without rebuilding the entire database.

We're not the first to take this approach.

CockroachDB eventually replaced RocksDB with Pebble, a storage engine written in Go, partly to gain greater control over its implementation and optimization.

SolariumDB follows a similar motivation within the .NET ecosystem.

What's Next?​

SolariumDB is still young, and there's a significant difference between producing promising benchmarks and operating a reliable storage engine in production.

RocksDB will remain CamusDB's default storage engine while we continue testing, benchmarking, and hardening SolariumDB.

Durability, recovery, and predictable behavior are non-negotiable. A faster database isn't useful if it cannot reliably preserve your data.

Our goal is to mature SolariumDB into a strong alternative while gaining deeper visibility and control over the entire database stack.

Building a storage engine from scratch is a substantial investment, especially when excellent alternatives already exist.

But sometimes the motivation isn't to replace something because it's broken.

It's to gain the freedom to understand, modify, and optimize every layer of the system.

entry.title: From 400 to 10,000 operations per second in CamusDB
entry.summary: What helped a three-node CamusDB cluster reach 10K ops/sec on one laptop, and how to interpret the result.
entry.content:
If you're investigating database throughput, our experience offers a practical place to look: the work repeated around every query and commit. Here's what we removed, how we measured the gains, and what the resulting benchmark can tell you about CamusDB.

Many months ago, when we first started measuring database throughput in cluster mode, we discovered it could only handle around 400 ops/sec. After a long journey of benchmarking, investigating bottlenecks, and optimizing the system, we've reached 10K ops/sec.

On October 12, a three-node cluster sustained 10,284 durable operations per second for 45 minutes, completing 27.8 million operations after a two-minute warm-up. Every measured minute stayed above 9,700 ops/sec.

All three nodes ran on one laptop, alongside the load generator and metrics collector. And the storage was memory-backed. Both details matter when interpreting the number.

What counts as an operation?​

We used Caraxes, our database testing tool, to run a bank ledger with 2,000 accounts. Half the operations read one account by its primary key. The other half transferred money: subtract from one account, add to another, and commit both changes together.

The read operation executes this parameterized query. @id is the account's primary key; the client consumes all four returned columns and checks that the requested account came back before counting the read as complete.

SELECT id, balance, version, payload
FROM workload_accounts WHERE id = @id;

A transfer moves one unit between two distinct accounts. The sequential client visits them in ascending row-index order, reading and updating each in turn. Here is the sequence, with parameter names expanded to distinguish the two accounts:

BEGIN;

/* account 1 */
SELECT balance, version FROM workload_accounts WHERE id = @low_id;
UPDATE workload_accounts
SET balance = @low_balance, version = version + 1 WHERE id = @low_id;

/* account 2 */
SELECT balance, version FROM workload_accounts WHERE id = @high_id;
UPDATE workload_accounts
SET balance = @high_balance, version = version + 1 WHERE id = @high_id;

COMMIT;

The client calculates each new balance from the value it read: subtract one from the sender and add one to the recipient. Either account can be the sender. Each update must match exactly one row, and incrementing version lets the verifier account for row changes afterward. The driver starts and commits the transaction through its API; BEGIN and COMMIT show those boundaries here.

One committed transfer counts as one operation, including both reads, both updates, and the commit. The result was approximately 5,140 standalone reads and 5,145 committed transfers per second.

Transfers selected accounts across the whole table, so concurrent transactions could modify the same rows. Conflicting work was retried. The run used read-committed isolation and 256 concurrent workers over 64 connections; each worker waited for its operation to finish before starting another.

Afterward, Caraxes reconciled the ledger. The total balance was unchanged, and no transaction had an indeterminate outcome: none left the client unsure whether it committed.

Three replicas, one hardware budget​

The host was an Intel Core i7-13620H laptop with 10 cores, 16 hardware threads, and 31 GiB of RAM, running Debian 12 and Docker.

The table had one replication group: a leader that ordered writes and two followers that maintained their own copies.

Every write goes through consensus: nodes agree on the ordered changes before those changes reach database storage. Some reads also require consensus coordination. Each write is stored three times, once per node. All that work competes for the same machine's resources.

The laptop's consumer NVMe drive changed its write behavior after roughly 30 GB of sustained writes.

Where the gains came from​

Send requests directly to the leader. Initially, the client could contact any node, which might forward the request. Teaching it which node led the data range removed that extra hop and produced a 1.97× improvement. Before optimizing the work inside a request, we shortened its route.

Reduce the cost of agreement. CamusDB uses Raft, a protocol for keeping replicas in agreement. Improvements to replication and follower queues reduced a replication round from about 2.31 ms to 1.56 ms, adding 8–9% in throughput. Briefly collecting writes into batches also helped several requests share replication work. Measuring the actual wait and wake-up time was essential; the configured delay alone did not describe the cost.

Write fewer log entries. Replicas record changes in a log so they can apply them in order. A change in Kahuna, the transactional storage layer under CamusDB, reduced the log entries per transfer from six to four. That removed work from the replication path for every committed transfer.

Schedule less work. Some storage reads could use a published snapshot of the latest state without entering a queue for the key. More targeted notifications also reduced scheduling overhead. Together, these changes cut thread-pool work items from 65 to 33 per client operation. A thread pool runs queued pieces of work; making it schedule fewer pieces left more CPU time for the operations themselves.

Avoid repeating primary-key lookups. A primary-key lookup first finds the row's internal identifier. Caching that identifier let later requests skip the index read. This reduced underlying storage reads per operation by 47% and CPU time per operation by 8%. The cache recorded 76.85 million hits, no misses after warm-up, and no stale identifiers during the run.

Increasing concurrency from 128 to 256 workers then added another 8% in throughput. Latency roughly doubled, while CPU cost per operation stayed unchanged. More concurrency helped use the capacity we had freed, with a clear cost to individual requests.

Measure the ideas that don't help, too​

Several plausible changes failed to improve the result. Setting the .NET thread-pool minimum to 64, 128, or 1,024 made no measurable difference. Client TLS showed no measurable CPU cost at the leader. Sending transaction requests through a pipelined client at 128 workers did not help either.

Those measurements narrowed the investigation. We could stop tuning those settings and focus on costs that moved throughput or CPU time per operation.

What this result means for your workload​

The final run's median read latency was 3.6 ms, with 99% completing within 18 ms. Median transfer latency was 36 ms, with 99% within 157 ms. Throughput needs those latency numbers beside it, especially when increasing concurrency makes individual operations slower.

The leader was the bottleneck, consuming about 8.5 CPU cores; each follower used roughly 1.53. Three separate machines would provide a different resource budget and add network latency between replicas. This run cannot predict that deployment's throughput.

The 2,000-row working set also fits comfortably in memory. It stresses transaction processing and contention, without measuring large-table scans or a database larger than RAM. Client traffic used cleartext gRPC; traffic between Raft peers retained certificate protection.

Correctness was checked beyond the throughput run. The same stack passed two two-hour fault tests involving killed leaders, paused processes, and severely throttled disks. Balances remained correct, replicas did not diverge, and no transactions remained unresolved across the tested restarts. The separate NVMe fault tests measured 3,230–5,485 ops/sec under their conditions.

The frozen campaign baseline was 407.86 ops/sec with the same workload shape and 32 workers. The final result is 25.2× higher, combining software changes with increased concurrency. It is a milestone for this workload and setup.

If you're profiling your own system, count the forwarding hops, log entries, queued tasks, and lookups behind each operation. Those repeated costs gave us concrete changes to make—and correctness checks told us whether the faster system still did the right work.

Conclusion​

Running three nodes on a single machine with commodity hardware is far from ideal and certainly not a recommended practice, since the shared hardware becomes a single point of failure for all three nodes. However, it demonstrates that even under these challenging conditions, the database can deliver performance that is more than adequate for the vast majority of transactional applications.

entry.title: A young database meets the Join Order Benchmark
entry.content:
If your queries join five, ten or fifteen tables, CamusDB now plans them better and runs them faster. This post explains what changed in plain terms, so you can see what to expect from your own queries.

A join query names its tables and its conditions. It does not say in which order to join the tables. The database picks the order, and the order decides how much data the query reads. A good order starts from the few rows that survive the filters. A bad order can build millions of rows and then throw most of them away.

The Join Order Benchmark (JOB) is a set of 113 queries from a 2015 paper by Leis and five co-authors. The queries run over a movie database of 21 tables, and each one joins 4 to 17 tables. The paper tested mature databases and found that their estimates of how many rows a join returns were often wrong by orders of magnitude. The error grows with each join, and a wrong estimate leads to a slow plan. The benchmark exists to show that weakness.

Where we started​

In July I wrote about how CamusDB searches for a join order. In short, the planner finds the cheapest plan for small groups of tables first and reuses those plans for larger groups.

Our first run of the 113 JOB queries used synthetic movie data at 1/1000 of the real size. SQLite ran the same rows as an independent check. Every CamusDB result matched. But 25 queries did not finish in 30 seconds, and the full run took 1,159 seconds. Every plan contained a cross product, a join of every row against every row.

The executor was fine. We put the tables of two queries in a good order by hand. One query went from 10 seconds to 0.4 seconds. Another went from a timeout to 40 milliseconds. The planner did not find the order on its own.

What changed​

Six changes made the difference. Each one stands on its own, and each one applies to every join query, not only to the benchmark.

The planner reads every condition on its own. A JOB query lists its tables with commas and puts all conditions in WHERE. The old planner grouped the conditions as the query wrote them. A table whose only link came through a later table looked unconnected, so the planner joined it with a cross product. The planner now reads each condition on its own and finds the links between tables wherever they are. No JOB plan has a cross product today. The run went from 1,159 seconds to 184 seconds, with no timeouts.

One estimate per group of tables. To compare two orders, the planner estimates how many rows each step produces. JOB queries name the same movie through up to six columns and write every pair of them as equal. The old estimator treated each of those fifteen equalities as a separate filter and multiplied the estimate down to almost nothing. The new estimator sees one fact: these six columns hold the same value. The run went from 184 seconds to 9.5 seconds.

Wide joins get the full search. The search compares every group of tables that an order can build. That number grows fast, so the old search stopped at 12 tables and used a simple rule above that. Nine JOB queries have 14 or 17 tables. The search now skips the groups that no order can build, which are most of them, and plans joins of up to 30 tables. Past a budget of steps it takes a fast greedy order instead of a slow search.

Statistics that see popular values. The planner sizes a join from the number of distinct values in the join column. That formula assumes every value is as common as every other. Real data is not like that: one movie has thousands of cast rows and most have a few. ANALYZE now keeps the most common values of each column with their counts, and the planner uses them. It also records how many rows hold NULL, because a NULL key joins with nothing. When a query filters a small lookup table down to one row, the planner reads that row before it plans. It then prices the join by the popularity of that key.

Each lookup costs less. With a good order, a join runs as a chain of index lookups. For each row on the left, the join finds the rows on the right that match. The old lookup asked the store for a page of 512 index entries and used 11 of them on average. The lookup now stops at the entries of its key. The join also keeps the rows of each key it found, so a repeated key costs nothing. And it sends a page of left rows to the store in one request instead of one request per row.

A test that watches plan quality. A correctness test does not catch a planner that returns the right rows and reads ten times more data to do it. A new test suite runs a fixed set of queries on fixed data and counts the rows and lookups of each plan. It compares the counts with a baseline file in git and fails when a query's work grows by more than half. The JOB queries run every night, and every result is checked against SQLite.

The numbers​

Work is the number of rows read, key lookups and index entries scanned over the whole plan, at a scale of about 225,000 rows.

BaselineTotal work, 113 queriesLargest estimate error
First baseline6,111,33678,378x
Current1,007,7521,240x

The engine does one sixth of the work it did at the first baseline, for the same results. The same test on the same laptop ran the 113 queries in 51 seconds before the lookup changes and runs them in 7.9 seconds today. No query takes more than a second. The three 17-table queries took 4 to 5 seconds each and now run in under 15 milliseconds.

The plan quality page in the docs compares the three engines on the same rows with warm runs. CamusDB takes 1.5 seconds, SQLite 7.2 seconds and PostgreSQL 0.74 seconds. CamusDB runs as an embedded node on a transactional key-value store, so this is a reference and not a race. Before this work, 25 of these queries did not finish at all.

Why this matters outside a benchmark​

Each change answers a problem that real tables have. The benchmark only made them visible at the same time.

The shape of a JOB query is common. One large table links to many small ones, and the filters sit on the small ones. That is a star schema, and most applications have one:

  • An online store joins orders to customers, products, categories, warehouses and shipments. A report filters on one category or one month.
  • A ledger joins transactions to accounts, counterparties, currencies and instruments. A statement filters on one account and a date range.
  • A multi-tenant product joins events to tenants, users, projects and plans. Every query filters on one tenant.
  • A game backend joins players, inventories, items, trades and guilds. A player's screen filters on one player.

The data behind those tables is skewed, has NULLs, and repeats its keys:

  • A few products appear in most orders. A few accounts hold most of the transactions. One tenant can hold half of the rows. A planner that prices every value alike plans for the average and then meets the largest customer.
  • Foreign keys are often NULL: an order without a coupon, a transaction without a counterparty, an item without an owner. An estimate that ignores NULLs is wrong by the NULL share.
  • Keys repeat. Every line of an order carries the same order id, and every row of an inventory carries the same owner. A lookup that remembers its answers runs once per key.
  • Nobody writes a FROM list in the best order, and an ORM or a report builder writes it in no order at all. The planner has to find it.

The last point matters most for CamusDB. The store is distributed, so each lookup can be a network round trip. A plan that looks up a thousand times where ten would do is slow by the latency of the cluster.

What a robust optimizer means here​

A benchmark win can hide a fragile optimizer. These are the properties I care about more than the time:

  1. Results never change. SQLite checks every plan on every nightly run. A plan that changes results is a bug, not an optimization.
  2. The search is bounded. The step budget and the greedy fallback keep planning time small at any width. The 17-table queries plan in 9 to 16 milliseconds.
  3. The same query gets the same plan. Two orders of equal cost keep the order the user wrote.
  4. No statistics means a fallback, not a failure. Without statistics the planner uses a simple order and still removes avoidable cross products.
  5. The plan is visible. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) shows the order the search chose, its estimate next to the actual rows, and the lookups each join saved.
  6. Regressions are caught before merge. The plan quality test runs on every pull request.

What is still open​

PostgreSQL executes the corpus five times faster, and the gap is in the executor, not in the planner. The search considers one shape of plan, a chain that adds one table at a time. Plans that join two groups of tables, and a search below an outer join, are not there yet. The worst estimate error is still above 1,000x on one query.

A young database does not win a benchmark. It learns from one. JOB told us where the optimizer was wrong, in a form we could measure and gate. That is the victory I want to keep.

entry.title: What the dragon found, part three
entry.summary: A dragon breaking one artic city of glowing pyramids
entry.content:
A ten-minute test finds the bugs that happen in ten minutes.

A distributed database is hard to build, and the code is the smaller half of the work. The larger half is verification. You check the results again and again, you dig into the system until you know what it really does, and you push it past the point where it should break. A guarantee on a documentation page is worth exactly what the evidence behind it can show, and that evidence has to cover speed and correctness at the same time.

Part one introduced Caraxes, the harness that attacks a real CamusDB cluster in Docker. Part two told what it found in its first month: a dropped transfer leg, a cluster that said healthy while it was dead, scans that lost rows under load.

This part covers the three weeks after that. Most of it is about one test. It runs for two hours, it injects a fault every eight minutes, and it took eight attempts before it passed. Every failed attempt found something, and the runs after the first pass kept finding things.

Three weeks, in numbers​

CamusDB still runs on two lower layers. Kahuna is the replicated key-value store under the SQL engine. Kommander is the Raft implementation under Kahuna. A chaos run attacks all three at once.

RepositoryCommits since 2026-09-21Versions consumed by CamusDB
CamusDB116
Kahuna100from 1.9.2 to 1.11.10
Kommander68from 1.7.6 to 1.10.9
Caraxes25
.NET client26

Caraxes now has 332 scenario files, up from about 200. More than thirty of the runs in this period were two hours long. That is more than sixty hours of a cluster under attack, on one host, with the same seed.

Why two hours​

Every ten-minute scenario in part two passed on the stack we shipped at the time. In those runs, node memory climbed to between 3.3 and 3.9 GB of a 4 GiB limit within ten minutes and then stayed there. Whether that plateau holds for two hours, or creeps, is a question no ten-minute run can answer. Snapshot installs, log compaction and retention floors are also things that only start to matter when the log is tens of millions of entries long.

So we wrote the soak. Three nodes with 4 GiB each, one partition replicated three times, the bank workload from part two with 128 workers over 2,000 rows, and a two-hour measured window. Fourteen faults land one every eight minutes. Six of them kill the current leader and restart it 30 seconds later. Four freeze a process for 30 seconds. Four pause one node's disk at 4 KiB per second for 30 seconds.

nemesis:
  seed: 1
  events:
    - { at: 8m,   fault: kill,      target: leader, duration: 30s }
    - { at: 16m,  fault: slow-disk, target: camus1, duration: 30s }
    - { at: 24m,  fault: kill,      target: leader, duration: 30s }
    - { at: 32m,  fault: pause,     target: camus2, duration: 30s }
    # ... fourteen windows in all ...
    - { at: 104m, fault: pause,     target: leader, duration: 30s }
    - { at: 112m, fault: kill,      target: leader, duration: 30s }

A soak passes when all of these hold:

  • The window completes, and no node dies on its own.
  • The sum of all balances is exactly 2,993,071,553 at the end, the same number as in part two.
  • Every indeterminate write is resolved. An indeterminate write is a commit whose answer the client never received, because the connection was cut while the commit travelled. The ledger resolves them afterwards: the sum of all row versions must land inside a band whose floor is the committed writes and whose ceiling adds the indeterminate ones.
  • The per-row ledger, joined against the seeded data, names no lost, missing, duplicated or half-applied row.
  • No two replicas applied the same log entry with different verdicts.
  • Every fault window recovers, and the cluster makes progress inside every window.

Throughput gates are not what the soak is for. The host's NVMe changes regime after 30 to 35 GB of writes, as part two explained, and a two-hour run always crosses that line. The harness marks a throughput finding inadmissible when the device moved inside the window, and most windows after minute 30 are. The verdict rests on the correctness checks, which do not depend on the device.

Since late September every soak runs as a pair. One arm has the new settle path on, where a transaction's resolved values are installed on every replica when the transaction settles. The other arm has it off, so a replica can keep a reference to the intent and fill in the value later. We call those by-reference records. The settle path writes 4.0 Raft entries per commit instead of 6.4, and it is the default today. Both arms must pass.

Run one: two nodes die, and the first three diagnoses are wrong​

The first soak completed its window: 17.9 million operations in two hours. It also finished with one node alive, and the reconciliation could not read the sum.

The first node died at minute 51. It was the leader, it was killed on schedule, it restarted, and it ran out of memory while it deserialized the backfill from the new leader. The runtime terminated it on purpose, with a message that said the orchestrator would restart it. Nothing did, because the harness only restarts a node as part of a kill fault, and that fault had already healed. The second node died after the window closed, while the reconciliation tried to read the sum from a two-node cluster. It was at 99.6 percent of its memory limit, with no trace and no dump. The kernel killed it.

The memory was real. What it was took four runs to find.

SuspectTestResult
Transaction record retention. The heap valve logged 185,064 resident records.Read the node metricsThe retention stores peaked at 117 to 131 MB per node, about 3 percent of the container, and held flat. Wrong.
RocksDB block cache and memtablesfs2: one shared budget of 768 MiB for both storage enginesNative memory unchanged at about 3 GB per node. A node died at minute 36, earlier than before. Wrong.
Index and filter blocks of the Raft log, kept outside every cacheMeasured at 8.9 percent of live SST bytes in a probe. Fixed in Kommander, with new gauges. fs3.Table readers read 0 MB. Native memory still 3,069 MB. The live SST was 262 MB, not the 34 GB the ratio implied. Wrong.
glibc malloc arenasRead the process maps on a live node116 anonymous mappings of 60 to 70 MB each, 1,227 MB resident. The process ran 133 threads on 16 cores, right at the allocator's ceiling of eight arenas per core.

glibc is the C library under .NET on Linux. Its allocator keeps a memory arena per thread, and freed memory stays in the arena. It does not return to the kernel. No subsystem gauge could find that memory, because it was not any subsystem's live data.

The fourth soak ran with one environment variable added, MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2. The 60 MB mappings fell from 116 to 7.

Nodefs3 peakfs4 peak
camus14,095 MiB, 100%3,463 MiB, 85%
camus24,000 MiB, 98%2,947 MiB, 72%
camus33,957 MiB, 97%3,268 MiB, 80%

No node died. Memory came down between faults, with no creep. Three soaks died of this, and the remedy was a deployment variable, not a change in either codebase. The fix for the Raft log's index blocks stays anyway. It bounded an allocation that had no bound, and its gauges are what made the measurement possible.

One native memory table from the first run says why the first diagnosis was wrong. On the node that died last, the working set grew from 382 MB to 4,057 MB over two hours, while the managed heap shrank from 767 MB to 441 MB. Read the difference between those two numbers before you blame anything the garbage collector manages.

The wedge under the memory wall​

With the deaths out of the way, the fourth soak showed a worse defect.

An hour into the window, with no fault active, client throughput went from 2,160 operations per second to zero in one second. It stayed at zero for 59 minutes. All three nodes were alive and answered every health probe.

All three voters shared a hole in their Raft log. The log was contiguous through entry 48,266,403, and entries were present up to 48,266,486. Neither recovery path could get past the hole:

  • One node won a term and refused to lead on the hole guard. It did that 598 times.
  • Another node won a term and its promotion barrier timed out. It reverted 297 times.
  • The third node never led. Terms climbed to 614. One node logged that the leader could not be resolved 167,244 times.

The trigger was a transient disk stall on one follower that cleared in seconds. The wedge outlived it by an hour.

This was not a new defect. The Kommander Jepsen suite found it in August, and its findings file recorded 90 nightly runs since then without a reproduction. This was its first reproduction outside Jepsen, on a far newer build, from ordinary device jitter rather than an injected fault. The soak also carried two details the Jepsen runs did not have. The refusal counter reset on every promotion attempt, so the truncation escape hatch could never fire. And 296 of the 297 barrier timeouts named no cause, while the real obstacle was the shared hole. Kommander 1.7.7 fixed it, and the next soak had no wedge.

A replica that came back with less than it left with​

The fifth soak ran on the published Kommander 1.7.7. No wedge, no node death, peak memory 55 percent. And the cluster stopped before minute 50 anyway, with all three nodes alive.

Minutes0-1010-2020-3030-4040-5050-6060-7070-9090-120
Ops/s5,0864,3102,2254,4801,7555943031-85

The leader was killed at minute 24 and rejoined. The new leader escalated to a snapshot install, and chunk 22 of 23 was rejected after a 16-second install. Within 41 seconds the node's checkpoint jumped ahead of the gap. The retry at that index was answered "already covered, nothing was imported".

From then on, that node held committed values for fewer rows than its peers at the same applied log position: 1,828 rows, then 1,777, then 1,756 of 2,000. Kahuna's fingerprint probe caught the difference three times at error level. The probe only logged, so the node was elected leader twice with the incomplete state. It also kept 172 prepared intents that the other two replicas settled long before. Under retention pressure those intents lost their records, and recovery must hold a record-less intent forever. 86 transactions' keys went read-only, workers piled onto them, and every full-table scan failed its page budget. The reconciliation could not read the table.

The sixth soak, on Kahuna 1.9.7 and Kommander 1.7.9, showed the same defect on a different node, after a snapshot install that completed cleanly with no chunk rejected. So the loss survives a clean install. The seventh soak ran a local Kommander fix for the skip. Same divergence, after two full installs, and this time no kill was involved: the leader stepped down on its own during a disk stall, with a hole in its own log.

Three Kommander changes closed it:

  1. A skip must deliver the committed entries below the index, or it must become an install.
  2. The installer skips the import when the application already applied past the index. An import there rewound state below the apply cursor, and those entries were never re-delivered.
  3. The leader does not escalate to a snapshot for a peer that already reports committed through the checkpoint.

The eighth soak passed. It was the first complete, clean two-hour window: conservation exact, 2,912 indeterminate writes all resolved, zero divergence, all fourteen windows recovered in at most 0.8 seconds. The ninth soak repeated it on published packages, Kahuna 1.9.9 and Kommander 1.8.0. That run matters more than the eighth, because it hit the exact shapes that wedged runs five to seven three times. One node went through a rejected chunk, a forced install and a 24-chunk re-install, and was then elected leader three times with no divergence and no held intents.

Kahuna 1.9.11 then added containment. A replica whose apply projection diverges from its peers is gated: it gives up leadership, withholds its candidacy, and is re-seeded. Live intents are part of the fingerprint now, and a record-less hold is cross-checked with peers. The tenth soak passed with the containment in the build and silent, which is what it should be with nothing to contain.

RunStackResultWhat it found
fs1Kahuna 1.9.3, Kommander 1.7.6Two nodes dead, no verdictNative memory grew while the managed heap shrank
fs2Same, with a 768 MiB storage budgetOne node dead at minute 36Not the block cache
fs3Raft log index blocks charged to the cacheOne node dead at minute 85, sum exactNot the table readers. Allocator arenas.
fs4MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2No deaths. Leaderless for 59 minutes.Three voters shared one hole in the log
fs5Kahuna 1.9.4, Kommander 1.7.7Read-only wedge by minute 50A replica rejoined with about 10 percent of its rows behind, and led twice
fs6Kahuna 1.9.7, Kommander 1.7.9SameThe loss survives a clean install
fs7Local Kommander skip fixSame, with no kill involvedAn import below the apply cursor rewound state
fs8Three Kommander changes, localPassThe first clean two hours
fs9Kahuna 1.9.9, Kommander 1.8.0PassRepair paths exercised three times, no divergence
fs10Kahuna 1.9.11, Kommander 1.8.2PassContainment in the build, silent

The rest of the chain​

We ran the soak again on every new stack after it passed, and it found more. None of them was a lost write on a published package. Several of them were one step away from it.

A candidate that discarded valid votes. The eleventh soak paused the leader's process for 30 seconds, and the cluster completed zero operations for all 30. One survivor campaigned in terms 72 through 78. The other granted its vote every time. The candidate discarded every grant, because it re-checked the voter's log by index only, while the voter judged by term and index. Each grant also put the voter into its post-vote cooldown, so it never campaigned itself. The partition had no leader until the paused node woke up. The same discarded-vote line appeared 4 times in fs9 and zero times in fs8 and fs10, so the condition depends on timing and a soak alone cannot prove it gone. Kommander now judges a grant by the voter's own rule, and a deterministic test holds the shape.

A veto that arrived late. One error line grew with every build: 2 or 3 per node in fs3, 21 in fs8, 47 in fs9, 78 distinct transactions in fs10. The ledger found zero lost writes every time, so it sat on the watch list. The cause was a prepare re-driven to a successor after a step-down. Its first copy had already settled, and the re-driven copy installed a phantom intent that the fence then refused against the transaction's own commit. Kahuna now remembers settled identities from the log, and the count went from 78 to zero.

The faster commit path broke the retention floor. A Kommander change that fans a proposal out before the leader's local write took one fsync out of every round. On this host's device that is 5,292 operations per second against 2,243 on the same body. It also turned the log retention budget of one million entries from 80 seconds of log into 37. A leader killed for 30 seconds came back 1.7 million entries behind, below the compaction floor, and needed a whole-partition transfer. The import ran out of memory. Retention is sized in time as well as entries since Kommander 1.9.2, and that soak passed at 4,235 operations per second, with 6,971 in its first ten minutes before the device changed regime.

An install loop with a 15-second deadline. On Kahuna 1.10.5 a restarted leader entered a snapshot install loop. The last chunk's install took longer than the 15-second acknowledgement deadline on a busy device. The retry started a new export at a new index instead of a resume. The follower rejected the retry while its own install was in progress. Six attempts in four minutes, and the node's memory went from 1.15 GB to 4.08 GB in three and a half minutes, then it crashed. The same loop ran in the previous soak and finished on the second to fourth attempt, with memory at 96.6 percent. The margin was between 100 and 300 MB. The settle-path arm of the same pair landed five of six installs on the first attempt in 8 to 15 seconds, because its snapshot carries fewer intents. A smaller snapshot hid the race, and did not fix it.

Lost writes, twice, on local packs. The packs that fixed the loop lost committed writes. In the first run the sum came back short by 4. Two rows were 58 and 180 version increments behind, about 100 seconds of each row's writes. The restarted node received a checkpoint over its replication gap. The leader escalated to a snapshot at exactly that index, the receiver answered "already covered, nothing was imported", and the leader moved its cursors past the gap. The node led one minute later. The entries between its frontier and the boundary never reached its application. In the second run the sum was short by 2, from a different cause. On restart, the node replayed the window below its certified position as history, and 82,536 by-reference records on all 2,000 keys found no intent to resolve against. The values were missing on that one node. The control arm, with the settle path on, on the same packs and the same schedule, passed. One variable, one answer.

A gate that fired nine minutes late. With the replay fixed, the next soak passed, and one of its six restarts left 10,773 unresolved records on 13 keys. Kahuna's new recovery gate caught it nine minutes later, after the node had won three terms. The node refused to serve, handed leadership to the fuller replica, re-seeded in 19.6 seconds and ungated. No loss. Nine minutes is too long, so the gate now fires at detection, and the next pair passed on both arms with the unresolved counter at zero on six restarts.

A paused follower re-seeded three times. The soak on the published Kahuna 1.11.5 and Kommander 1.10.4 passed on both arms, and both arms showed the same thing. A 30-second pause at minute 104, with 60 to 70 million entries in the log, was followed by three consecutive whole-partition re-seeds: 32, 38 and 31 chunks in 60, 41 and 8 seconds, with the follower at 92 percent of its memory during the first. The first diagnosis said the follower fell below the compaction floor. The code said otherwise. The retention window covered it by an order of magnitude. The backfill's no-progress probe counted four shipments fruitless because the follower's reported commit frontier did not move, while its presence frontier advanced at 1,100 entries per second against a stream of 6,700. Each install left the follower a million entries behind, and the probe fired again. With the probe reading every frontier, the same pause was repaired by backfill: 92,000 entries behind to 13 in 28 seconds. Kommander 1.10.7 ships it, and in the latest soak the minute-104 pause hit the leader, which caught up from 188,000 entries behind to 3,000 in three minutes with no escalation.

sn3Local, replay fixedPassThe recovery gate caught 10,773 unresolved records, nine minutes late

When the dragon was wrong, again​

Part two had a section with this name. Here is the new list. Every item cost us a wrong reading once, and every item is a check now.

  • A node that died on its own, twice, did not. In one run the health probe was issued 0.28 seconds before the scheduled SIGKILL, and the harness graded the missed probe as a death with no fault active. In another, docker kill took 6.8 seconds to return on a device at 98 percent busy, and the harness opened the fault window when the command returned, seven seconds after the node died. Fault windows now open when the fault is issued, and a probe in flight within its own timeout before a window is excused. Both runs re-grade as passes on recorded data.
  • 801 version increments above the band were the band's unit. One run's version sum exceeded the ceiling that the indeterminate writes allowed. The ceiling counted one row per indeterminate transaction. A transfer increments two rows. With the right unit the sum was inside the band and the excess above the floor was even, so every transfer applied whole. We replayed the corrected band over 410 archived runs. Thirty runs that had read "above the maximum" were inside. One run from August 28, with zero indeterminate writes and a conserved balance, grew the version sum by 8: four transfers applied that the client never committed. The check was waived under faults at the time, and the waiver hid it. The band is graded in bank mode now, and an odd excess fails as a half-applied transfer.
  • An Elle history with holes in it. On Docker Desktop for macOS the workload wrote its history through a bind mount, and every time a fault started a helper container, a page-aligned run of zero bytes appeared in the host copy. Elle could not parse the history, so one scenario never had a verdict. The measured run now writes inside its container and the harness copies the output out.
  • A node that left the cluster, except it did not. The node-removal fault posted its leave request from the host. The request arrived through Docker's port proxy from the bridge gateway, and the node refused it, because cluster administration over the network requires authentication. The vacuity check described below caught it: a run that promised replica moves had none. The request now runs from inside the target's own network namespace.
  • A clock library that broke sleep. The first clock-skew shim was libfaketime. Under .NET 10 it made timed waits return at once, so the test subject was a database with no timers. The shim is now a small C library that moves the wall clock and leaves monotonic time alone.
  • A client check on one sample. A soak with every database signal clean failed on the load generator's thread-pool queue, which peaked at 103 against a bar of 100 for one second. The rule now judges the queue on dwell time and the 95th percentile. In the same run a fault aimed at the leader was skipped, because one placement sweep taken mid-election saw no leader. The resolver now sweeps every half second for up to ten seconds.
  • An idle disk probe that predicted nothing. We waited up to three hours for the host's idle fsync latency to drop below a threshold before a soak. It read 2.4 to 3.1 ms the whole time on a rebooted idle host, and the run then opened at 0.05 ms anyway. The in-run regime rules are the signal. The gate is gone.

A test that did nothing must not pass​

A fault that never fires leaves a green run behind. The node-removal item above was found by a rule we added for exactly that reason. A scenario can now declare that it requires a range split, or a replica move, and the harness fails the run as vacuous when the placement samples show neither happened.

That rule guards four new scenarios. Two run key-range sharding, where a table is split into ranges by key and the ranges move between nodes as they grow. The seeded data starts a cascade of splits that outlasts the warm-up, and a partition and a kill land while ranges still split. Two run replica placement on five nodes with three replicas each: a kill at 25 seconds, then a decommission at 80 seconds that drains every replica the node hosts onto the others, so the cluster finishes the run with four nodes. Each pair has an Elle arm, which looks for isolation anomalies in a list-append history, and a bank arm, where the conserved sum and the per-row ledger see a row that a split copy or a seeded replica lost.

Both features are opt-in. The consistency report listed them as the two weakest verified parts of the system. They now have CamusDB-level scenarios that run every night.

Clocks, and the nightly​

Part one promised clocks that disagree between nodes. Caraxes can now move one node's wall clock forward or back, by up to twelve hours, and move it back on heal. Only the wall clock moves, so the fault reaches the hybrid logical clock and every lease built on it, and not Raft, whose elections use monotonic time.

Four scenarios target what a given skew can reach: 2 seconds on three nodes as a control, a jump past the 5-second snapshot clock fence, a jump past the 15-second intent and prepare lease, and 3 minutes forward then 1 minute back, past the gossip and schema leases. All four passed with a serializable Elle history. One change came out of them: Kahuna now refuses a snapshot read whose timestamp leads the node's clock, and no longer serves it unfenced.

Caraxes also has CI now. Tests run on every push. Every night at 05:00 UTC a workflow builds CamusDB from main and runs the ten Elle list-append scenarios, one job per scenario. The nightly runs in a correctness-only mode: the recovery-time and throughput rules are reported as not graded, because a hosted runner's speed says nothing about the change. Elle, the ledger, the divergent-apply check, node health and the total-outage rule still grade the run.

Notes from the performance side​

The harness is also how we measure speed, and three of its findings in this period were about the measurement or the client, not the server.

  • TLS was never the cost. A pair of ten-minute runs on one image, with the client path in TLS and in cleartext, read 9,082 and 9,240 operations per second at an identical 0.90 CPU-milliseconds per operation on the leader. Cleartext is now the control shape. Raft keeps its certificate.
  • A pipelined client that landed on the wrong node. The new client sends a transfer as two frames instead of six exchanges. Its first measurement was 5,029 operations per second against 9,236 for the sequential client. A pipelined statement carried no routing negotiation, so two thirds of first frames began on a follower, and follower CPU per operation went up four times. With routing fixed in client 0.15.1 the pipelined arm reads 5,737. The second frame, two updates and a commit, costs 27.9 ms against 13.6 ms for the same statements sent one by one. That question is open.
  • A thread pool with a floor of 1,024. Scheduler statistics put 6.8 of the leader's 8.3 cores in 233 to 284 pool workers, at 29 to 33 time slices per client operation, on a host with 16 hardware threads. The server's default minimum of 1,024 threads is what lets the pool grow that far. The pair at a floor of 64 and 128 is the next run.

What the database looks like today​

  • A node that runs out of memory was a deployment problem. Every Caraxes node runs with MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2, the Raft log's index blocks are charged to the shared storage budget, and node memory peaks between 80 and 93 percent of 4 GiB over two hours and comes down between faults.
  • A partition whose voters share a hole in the log elects a leader.
  • A replica that diverges is contained. It gives up leadership, withholds its candidacy, and is re-seeded. A restart that leaves unresolved by-reference records gates at detection, before the node can win a term.
  • A snapshot install cannot skip over a gap, an import cannot rewind below the apply cursor, and a leader does not re-seed a peer that catches up on its own.
  • A vote is judged by term and index on both sides.
  • Log retention is sized in time as well as entries, so a faster commit path does not shrink the window a 30-second restart needs.
  • A re-driven prepare whose first copy settled is rejected, instead of installed as a phantom.

The last pair on a published stack, Kahuna 1.11.7 and Kommander 1.10.7, is double green.

CheckSettle path offSettle path on
Conservationexactexact
Lost rows, divergent applies, unresolved records0, 0, 00, 0, 0
Faults recovered14 of 1413 of 13
Longest recovery0.9 s0.7 s
Snapshot installs00
Pauses repaired by backfill4 of 43 of 3
Memory peak90%90%

The settle-path arm injected thirteen faults, not fourteen. One pause aimed at the leader was skipped by the resolver bug listed above, which is fixed since.

CamusDB today pins a Kahuna three releases past that pair. The pin is ahead of its evidence, as it was in part two, and the next soak closes that gap.

Three lessons​

Some bugs need two hours. Every ten-minute run in part two plateaued at 3.3 to 3.9 GB and passed. In hindsight those plateaus were the memory wall, a few hundred megabytes away. A plateau is not evidence of a bound. Only a long run with the same budget is.

Measure the quantity. Do not infer it from a ratio. The table-reader ratio of 8.9 percent was right, and the SST volume it was multiplied against was never measured. The inference said 34 GB. The gauge said 262 MB. Two subsystem hypotheses failed in a row for the same reason, and the one that held came from reading the process maps.

Change one thing. The sum came back short by 2 on a pack that changed two things. The control arm with the settle path on, same pack, same schedule, passed, and that isolated the loss to the by-reference replay in one run. Three soaks died of memory, and the fix was one environment variable with no code change. A result you cannot attribute to one variable is a story, not a finding.

Part two's third lesson held as well. The chain from the first soak to the latest is memory, then a wedge, then a divergence, then a livelock, then an install loop, then two lost writes, then a re-seed storm. Every fix uncovered the next failure when it removed the one in front of it.

This is what most of the engineering on a distributed database looks like. Not new features, but a long check that the ones we promised still hold, under faults, under load, for hours, on a real device. A database earns its guarantees twice, once in the code and once in the evidence, and the second time never ends. The soak is that second time, for performance and for correctness in the same run.

The dragon is not done. The next runs are the kill matrix under load, a second kill window measured on a device that holds its regime, and the two open questions from the performance side. But a server that dies on a busy afternoon now dies on a build that survived fourteen of those afternoons in a row, twice, with the sum exact at the end.

entry.title: What the dragon found
entry.summary: A dragon breaking one pyramid in a city of glowing pyramids
entry.content:
In a world that's moving faster every day, where software verification is essential to keep up with that pace, building increasingly specialized harnesses, simulators, and test suites has become imperative.

A few weeks ago, we introduced Caraxes, our test suite for simulating extreme scenarios and pushing the database to its limits under all kinds of conditions: node failures, network issues, disk contention, and more.

The results have been extremely valuable, helping us uncover issues in both performance and correctness.

It's similar to putting an F1 car through different configurations in a simulator before those failures happen during a race. It allows us to expose the system to hundreds of hours of testing and exceptional conditions, compressed into just a few hours.

This post is the second part. It tells what the dragon found, what we fixed, and how the database is more robust today.

One month, in numbers​

CamusDB runs on two lower layers. Kahuna is the replicated key-value store under the SQL engine. Kommander is the Raft implementation under Kahuna. A chaos run attacks all three at once, so a finding can land in any of them.

Between the first post and this one, the three repositories received a large amount of work. Most of it came from a Caraxes run that failed.

RepositoryCommits since 2026-08-19Releases consumed by CamusDB
CamusDB150
Kahunaabout 13345 versions, from 1.0.6 to 1.9.2
Kommanderabout 110from 1.2.x to 1.7.6

Caraxes itself has about 200 scenario files. Many of them carry a long header that reads like a lab notebook. The header records what the previous run showed, what changed for this run, and what result counts as a pass. The rest of this post is a walk through those notebooks.

The first real bug that money found​

The first post explained our strongest check. A workload moves money between random accounts, and the total of all balances must be exactly the same at the end. We call it the bank workload.

The first bank run that failed this check was a two-hour run, with random faults, on an early build. The sum went down by three units.

BeforeAfterDifference
2,993,071,5532,993,071,550-3

Three units out of three billion is a tiny number. It is also a proof that one transaction applied only half of a transfer. We spent days on this one.

The cause was in the SQL engine, not in the replication layer. When CamusDB reads a row from Kahuna, the answer can be a confirmed value, a confirmed absence, or a non-answer. A non-answer means the read timed out, or the key was in the middle of replication, or that key returned an error.

The read path treated the non-answer as an absence. From there, the failure was quiet at every step:

  1. The UPDATE for one side of the transfer looked for the row and found nothing.
  2. A match of zero rows is not an error, so the statement reported success.
  3. The transaction committed with one leg of the transfer missing.
  4. Commit validation saw nothing wrong, because the read recorded no observation to validate.

The fix is a contract that now applies to every read path in the engine: a read that cannot confirm the state of a key must fail the statement. It must never report absence. A regression test in the engine carries the run name and the missing three units in its comments.

We also added a tripwire in the workload. If an UPDATE matches zero rows right after a SELECT that found the row, the transfer throws. That way, the same class of bug appears as a loud failed transfer instead of a small drift in a sum.

A cluster that says healthy while it is dead​

The second finding is the one that changed how we read health checks.

A busy partition changed leader after a fault. The new leader started a backfill for a follower. A heartbeat acknowledgement with no report made the leader believe the follower was at entry one, so the backfill started at entry one. The follower's log was already compacted, so it refused. The refusal never escalated, and the partition stopped committing. Permanently.

During all that time, every node reported ready. The cluster health endpoint said three of three nodes up, healthy, for 83 minutes, while the workload made zero progress.

The fix in Kommander removed the fabricated anchor. Two more releases removed a side effect, where the refusal escalated into a full snapshot on every election. But the more important change was in how Caraxes and CamusDB judge health:

  • Caraxes detects a wedge by commit progress, never by node liveness. A window with zero operations during a fault fails the run.
  • CamusDB gained a degraded-partition detector. A partition whose leader has an open backfill refusal, or a snapshot rescue that never converges, is reported as degraded even while its healthy quorum keeps committing.
  • Caraxes now probes every node during the run and grades outages against the fault timeline. A node that dies while its container stays up fails the run. This rule exists because one run passed with a dead node inside a green container.

The same family produced smaller fixes. A snapshot install loop sent 76 installs to one follower in 13 minutes without convergence. A step-down that raced an in-flight proposal left callers with no reply, no failure, and no timeout. A node did not rejoin after a SIGSTOP pause. Each one was found by a run that stalled at a specific minute, with a specific seed, and was fixed against a repeat of that run.

One key, eight runs​

Not every bug falls in one run. The longest chain in the notebooks started with a 45-minute run named R and ended with a run named Z. Every run in the chain used the same seed, the same faults, and the same workload. Only the engine changed.

RunResultWhat we learned
RSum off by 81, durableA replica that held a write intent deferred its own transaction's materialization forever. Reads then served the older revision.
SSum off by 2The lost units were the first commit at the start of a wedge. The wedged key refused every write until the end of the run.
TSum off by 1, for 46 minutesThe new self-repair read from the wedged node's own state, which was itself behind, so it repaired nothing.
UPass, with two keys wedged read-onlyThe repair's single retry was lost in the same pause that caused the miss. Nothing re-armed it.
VCould not seedThe new armed repair turned a cheap false alarm into a storm: about 1,000 re-drives per node in under a minute.
WPassThe repair now verifies a miss off the actor before it acts.
XFail, same build as W38 rows were frozen up to 186 commits behind in scans, while the aggregates were fully caught up.
Y, ZPass, twiceA durable head that only moves forward. Zero refusal lines across all nodes for the whole window.

Two rules came out of this chain.

The first rule is that one clean window is not evidence. Run W passed and the identical run X failed. Now a build must pass two consecutive windows before we call it stable.

The second rule is that the aggregate cannot see a stale key. Run U conserved the sum exactly, while one row sat one commit behind on every node. Now the verdict reads the sum in two ways, through the aggregate and through a full row scan, and both must agree.

Scans that drop rows only while you write​

The post-run check counts rows on a quiet cluster. For weeks it passed every time. Then we added a probe that runs SELECT COUNT(*) on every gateway every few seconds during the load.

Under load, the count returned between 1,962 and 1,999 rows out of 2,000. On every gateway. A scan dropped a row that a point read returned. The row was resident, written after the page started, and a non-snapshot page evaluated it as a snapshot read, then dropped it on a miss from the archive.

The second half of the bug was in CamusDB. A read-only scan carried a transaction id, so the MVCC pin in Kahuna could abort a retried page. One arm of a device-pause run produced 365 aborts out of 399 read-only counts. Read-only statements now carry no transaction id.

A related finding was much louder. A pessimistic run with serializable isolation wedged the cluster. Two nodes each read more than 645 GiB from a data directory of 118 MB, and the cluster could not serve one aggregate thirty minutes after the load stopped. A prefix scan with a pinned read timestamp walked the full revision history of every key, and the bank workload leaves each hot row with hundreds of revisions.

The probe is now part of the verdict. A short count is never tolerated, and a run without the probe prints that fact next to its result, because a run that did not test scan visibility proves less than its pass suggests.

Memory that grows without a bug, and memory that grows with one​

The two-hour runs started to die at minute 88, then at minute 105. Nodes were OOM-killed, or entered a garbage collection spiral with the container up at 110% CPU and the REST port unreachable.

The first cause had no defect in it. The .NET runtime caps its heap at 75% of the container limit by default. The heap plus the native memory of the storage engine added up to more than the container. A node under load long enough to reach its budget died with nothing wrong in the code.

The second cause was ours. Fixed cache floors pinned about 700 MB in caches for a working set of a few megabytes. The floors now yield to a proportional share when the container is small, and every Caraxes node runs with an explicit heap budget of 60% of its limit.

After that, the memory findings became real leaks, and each one has a number.

FindingMeasuredFix
One retained async state machine per gateway request2,906,601 retained objects against 2,912,492 requests on one nodeConstant-memory stream bookkeeping. Live growth fell from 0.258 to 0.039 KiB per operation.
Raft log reclamation could not keep up with ingest277 MB to 1,153 MB in ten minutesThe reclaim floor advances to the true floor on every pass, instead of a fixed number of entries.
Raft log write-ahead files pinned by a column family that never flushed443 MiB to 2,709 MiB in ten minutes, per nodeMetadata column family made flushable, and a cap on total write-ahead size.
Durable transaction records retained by age onlyFilled a 2,458 MiB heap in about five minutes at 8,000 ops/sRetention budget by count and by bytes, plus a heap-pressure valve.

One line from the notebooks explains why memory matters more in a soak than in a benchmark. A faster commit path without a memory fix makes a long run worse, because the run reaches the memory knee sooner. In one pair of runs, 5.8 times the throughput bought a decay that started 3.3 times earlier.

The last row of the table hid a second bug. An out-of-memory exception swallowed inside a write-ahead log write left a follower reachable and healthy, with its queue pinned at 4,096 and zero batches for four minutes. The run continued on a reduced quorum. We call this the zombie rule now: a node whose write counter stops while the busiest node keeps writing disqualifies the run, because a cluster that lost a replica without a fault is not the cluster the test claims to measure.

The disk is a participant​

The first post listed a full disk as the only disk fault. That was not enough.

During long runs on the benchmark host, the NVMe device produced fsync excursions of up to 3.2 seconds under sustained load. An in-flight commit then waited past its 15-second finalize budget and returned an unresolved outcome to the client. Healthy followers logged the stalled leader as unavailable. Nothing crashed, and nothing was wrong with the network.

So Caraxes gained a slow-disk fault. It caps one node's block writes through the kernel's I/O controller, on demand, at a chosen rate. The default rate is a device pause: one 4 KiB write per second. The process, its network, and its peers stay healthy while every durable write waits at the block layer.

That fault drove three changes in the engine:

  • A leader steps down cleanly on its own disk pause, and a follower's disk pause is ridden out from the log.
  • Kahuna rides out a single node's disk pause without unknown outcomes.
  • A local watchdog detects a durable write that stalls, so a node whose disk stopped answering no longer looks healthy.

A related gate compared a build with single-fsync commit on and off, under kills and partitions, with three seeds. The first pass failed the off arm with real data loss: the sum was short by one, and one row was short by five with zero indeterminate attempts, so no ambiguity band could explain it. The on arm passed. We repeated the gate with three more seeds, because one failure and one pass cannot separate a flag that helps from a flag that got lucky. Single-fsync commit is the default today.

The same campaign hardened restarts. A node restarted under load could take a snapshot for a log that already covered the floor, and then livelock on a tombstone. A node that restarted while a peer was briefly unreachable crashed at startup. Both are now regular scenarios, not accidents.

Balanced requests are not balanced work​

A three-node run split its requests almost perfectly across the three gateways, at 33.4%, 33.3%, and 33.4%. The report called it distributed. In the same run, one node led every partition, and one disk did 100% of the durable write work. One node logged about 500,000 key-value entries while the other two logged fewer than 2,000.

The leader balancer was on. It planned six moves and reported five timeouts, and it never emitted a success at all. A transfer suggestion addressed to the node that runs the balancer took an in-process shortcut instead of the transport, and every one of those moves was dropped. The drop paths logged at debug level, so a balancer that failed five of six moves was silent at the default log level.

The transport shortcut is fixed, and a lagging transfer target is now caught up within a bounded wait. Caraxes now waits for leadership to spread before a capacity window opens, and it fails a run that opens with all leaders on one node. An even gateway share says nothing about which disk does the writes.

When the dragon was wrong​

A harness that attacks a database also attacks the truth about it. Several of the most useful entries in the notebooks are findings against the measurement, not against the database.

  • A twelve-table seed appeared to stall for six hours and eighteen minutes. Three node logs fell silent in the same second and resumed together. The first reading was a defect report against the database. The laptop had slept. Caraxes now compares a monotonic clock with wall time, and a run whose host slept fails without exception.
  • A dependency bump looked like it cost 38% of throughput. We rebuilt the same commit with one character changed, the dependency version, and the bump cost 6.2%. Four commits in CamusDB owned the rest. A bisect on one merge commit separated two candidates cleanly.
  • Two arms with byte-identical binaries differed by 1.36x, and run order predicted throughput with a correlation of -0.963. Two recorded findings were retracted. Every performance comparison now runs as interleaved pairs in the order base, candidate, candidate, base, and a pair that disagrees in direction is refused.
  • The host NVMe serves the first 30 to 35 GB of a run from a write cache, then changes regime. Where that boundary lands depends on what the previous run left in the cache. Caraxes now writes fsynced ballast during warm-up so every run measures the same regime.
  • A closed-loop run reported 1,182 ops/s with 29.994 requests in flight against a cap of 32. That number was a limit of the load generator, not of the server. The verdict now records the generator's own CPU and queue depth and can fail a capacity run whose client had no headroom.
  • The container memory figure from Docker counts page cache and kernel memory together with the process. A tool now splits it into cache, native, unused heap, and live data, so a growth curve says which component grew.

Each of these produced a check. The checks are cheap, and they protect every later run from a false alarm we already paid for once.

A tuning note that reads like a bug​

One finding deserves a separate mention, because it was neither a bug nor a false alarm. It was a knob nobody turned.

The write-ahead log on the leader never grouped commits. It wrote exactly one operation per batch at every concurrency from 32 to 256 workers. The group commit linger defaults to zero, and the cluster baseline never set it. A report to the Raft layer that the log does not coalesce, written from runs where coalescing was off, would be a bad filing.

The measurements that followed changed defaults:

KnobMeasuredDecision
Linger of 1, 3, or 5 msIdentical batches at full occupancyLeft alone. The linger is inert on a single hot partition by design.
Post-completion hold of 2 ms51 to 110 items per round at 128 workers, 6% more throughput, lower write p50Now the default.
Two or four in-flight batches per partition15 to 20% lower throughputDefault stays at one.
Direct reads in the storage engineLeader reads from 1 ms to 40 to 50 ms with the CPU idleShips off.

What the database looks like today​

The list of fixes is long. The shape of the database after them is easier to describe.

  • Unknown is never absent. A read that cannot confirm a key fails the statement. A commit whose transport failed after submission reports an unresolved outcome, and the client retries the same commit on the same handle, instead of a definite-looking error that hides a landed write.
  • A stale leader cannot write. Proposals carry an expected term, quorum checks are on by default, and a leader that lost quorum learns it.
  • A published commit index never runs ahead of durable storage. The checkpoint floor advances only when every entry below it is on disk.
  • A wedge is loud. Backfill refusals, non-converging rescues, and stalled durable writes are reported by the node, and the harness fails a run with zero progress under a fault.
  • Memory has budgets. Retention is bounded by count and bytes, batch streams use constant memory, and storage budgets derive from the real heap limit.
  • The disk can pause and the cluster survives, with no unknown outcomes for a single paused node.
  • Every crash leaves evidence. Crash dumps live outside the data volume, node logs are captured before teardown, and the harness records which build, which durability settings, and which host produced every number.

The scenarios from the first post still run, and their recovery numbers are the ones we compare from build to build.

ScenarioFaultPeak error rateRecovery after heal
Kill a node during transfersSIGKILL for 20 seconds100%5.5 s
Kill a whole zoneTwo nodes of six, 30 seconds100%4.1 s
Full diskData volume filled to the last byte, 15 seconds25%1.6 s

The full disk case is the one we like most. The node refused writes with a clean error, kept serving reads, and accepted writes again with no restart as soon as space came back.

Kommander also gained an in-process simulation with seeded faults, trace shrinking, and invariant checkers, and Kahuna can now start a multi-node cluster in one process with link blocks and restarts. Caraxes found the failures at the level of a real cluster in Docker. These simulators reproduce them in milliseconds inside a unit test, so a fix comes with a test that fails on the old code.

Three lessons​

Invariants beat logs. Every serious correctness bug in this post was found by a number that did not add up, and only then explained by a log. Engine-side analysis of the logs alone ran out of evidence more than once. A per-row ledger of every transfer, joined against the seeded baseline, is what turned a deficit we could count into a deficit we could attribute.

The measurement is part of the system under test. A sleeping laptop, a busy host, a write cache, and a saturated load generator all produced findings that looked exactly like database defects. Each false alarm cost us time once. Each one now costs a check that runs on every run.

A fix reveals the next bug. The chain from run R to run Z is eight fixes deep, and every fix uncovered the next failure by removing the one in front of it. This is not a sign that the database was worse than we thought. It is what progress looks like when the test is stronger than the code.

The dragon is not done. There are scenarios in the notebooks with questions still open, and a few new faults on the list. But a server that dies on a busy afternoon now dies in a way we studied, on a build that passed the same afternoon many times before.

entry.title: Player inventories are bank accounts
entry.content:
A player spends forty hours to earn a sword. Another player pays real money for a bundle of skins. A guild saves gold for three weeks to buy a fortress.

None of that is "game data" to the person who did it. It is time, money, and trust. When a backend loses an item, duplicates a currency, or shows two owners for one mount, the player does not read it as a bug. The player reads it as disrespect.

We run game backends on CamusDB today. This post explains why we treat every inventory and every wallet as a small bank account. It also explains why that decision leads to distributed transactions, not away from them.

What a game economy really is​

Strip the art away and a game economy is a ledger.

  • A wallet is an account with a balance that must never go below zero.
  • An inventory is a set of assets, and each asset has exactly one owner.
  • A shop purchase is a transfer: currency leaves one account, an item enters another.
  • A trade between two players is a transfer in both directions, at the same instant.
  • A guild bank is a shared account with many writers.
  • A season reward is a credit that must be granted exactly once.

These are the same rules a bank enforces. The amounts are smaller. The number of accounts is often larger. The rules are identical:

balance >= 0
one item -> one owner
one reward -> granted once
a trade completes for both sides, or for neither

A bank does not ask whether a rule deserves enforcement on a slow day. It enforces the rule on every day, because a single broken rule ends the trust of the customer. Games are not different. A player who loses one legendary item once tells everyone, and that player is often right to do so.

The argument for one thread​

There is a popular argument in the game backend world, and it deserves a fair statement before we answer it.

The argument goes like this. Coordination is expensive. A transaction that touches data on several machines needs network round trips. A transaction that waits on a network round trip holds its locks for a millisecond instead of a few microseconds. If two transactions touch the same hot row, the second one waits for the first. A single thread on a single machine can process a hot row hundreds of thousands of times per second. A distributed commit on that same row processes it about a thousand times per second. Therefore, the argument says, keep each region of the game world in one single-threaded shard. Keep the transactions local. Pass messages between shards asynchronously. Reserve distributed transactions for rare cases, or avoid them completely.

The physics in that argument is correct. A network round trip is slower than a cache line. A hot row is serial by nature. Nobody can make ten machines update one row faster than one machine can.

The conclusion is where the argument fails for games. It fails for three reasons.

Reason one: the valuable transactions cross the shard boundary​

The argument assumes that most transactions stay inside one shard, and that the transactions that cross shards are rare and unimportant. In a game economy, the opposite is true. Look at where the money is:

  • A trade between two players who met in different regions.
  • A deposit into a guild bank from a member who plays on another continent.
  • A marketplace sale, where the seller and the buyer are never in the same place.
  • A gift from one account to another.
  • A player who walks from one region to another with a full inventory.
  • A cross-server event that pays a reward to every participant.

Every one of these moves value across a boundary. They are less frequent than movement updates, yes. They are also the transactions with the most real money, the most player hours, and the most exploit attempts behind them. Rare is not the same as unimportant. In an economy, the rare transaction is often the one that matters most.

A shard model that makes local work fast and cross-shard work unsafe optimizes the transactions that nobody would miss. It leaves the transactions that everybody would miss to hand-written code.

Reason two: asynchronous messages between shards are where duplicates come from​

If two shards cannot commit together, a trade between them becomes a conversation. Shard A removes the sword and sends a message. Shard B receives the message and adds the sword. If B is down, A must remember to retry. If A crashes after the removal and before the send, the sword is gone. If the message is delivered twice, the sword exists twice. If a player logs out during the hand-off between regions, the inventory can exist on both regions, or on neither.

Every game developer with a few years of live operations knows this pattern, because every item duplication exploit in history has this shape. The fix is always the same: idempotency keys, outbox tables, and compensation steps. A reconciliation job then runs at night and files the differences into a spreadsheet. That is a distributed transaction protocol. The game team writes it under a release deadline, without a model checker. The team then writes it again for each new feature that crosses a boundary.

A database with distributed transactions does that work once, in one place, and tests it against node failures. The cost is a millisecond at commit. The alternative is a saga for every feature. We prefer to pay the millisecond.

Reason three: the hot key is a simulation problem, not a ledger problem​
